e-7049.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Defective Case
e-7049.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/1ead7e2a9fff08d6ec1d8e70c3f9f0c10729a4899227c53eabe7a5212feb1659.png)

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/36b5e6757a7849e9e405883da345dadfbcc3130b517d05e117f4fb6fb4338ae8.png)

what is the value of $a+b?$
e-7049.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/f9f940992f15a14e58f7eee0b8171e8e0e437787d6340618fcd1f23b84d333a8.png)

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda=-4$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/9a7426e0e17bb57e1a8bfb24dca5ca3a579809708af3055184f9cfc2728957bc.png)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/f3e3bae74afa48fd689bb48dc317af52e44914f9f35d32375463d3705268b377.png)

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda$ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $\mathbf v,$ the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

To find $\mathbf{w},$ we solve the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-4+4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4+4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/6e5c9442761d05d62ccc3ce56cbe09794e57b931987e3e4ef33d93d7cfb1e39f.png)

So, we obtain

$$
w_2 = 1.
$$

The variable $w_1$ is a free variable. Setting $w_1 = 0,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/6b54faff854b99c0c86b3de477cc2dde8b5a714bfc296c59ed6757f9bc250f77.png)

Therefore, the general solution is given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/96ee1e3a1af5c670b87cd06e406ac16b0fa9f5e5305b2fe95dc395c079d291da.png)

Finally, we see that $a=0, b=1,$ and $a+b=1.$

e-7050.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem in a Defective Case
e-7050.problem:
Solve the initial value problem
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/9459f772e062490c525f6c7bc083c02d0ed5dc3bc4c331f642653aa4f9bf5515.png)
*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda=3.$*
e-7050.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/df4b98b4799865dbf40e765bda0fa6176157139d99a62bd1febe48d7c4600c8c.png)

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda=3$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/8032d75d584838d0743f2e9217c25844af637d07261dd2d6a89add9df531fdb1.png)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/aa5146c331315952e36051be1126010bbcaf706f2cbc1c886c56b0e92b468fa4.png)

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda$ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $\mathbf v,$ the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1  \mathbf{v}e^{\lambda t} + c_2 (\mathbf{v}t e^{\lambda t} +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

To find $\mathbf{w},$ we solve the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1-3 & -8 \\ 2 & 7-3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-4 & -8 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/b0d075668031a0decad6d092f2f03c3f74eacdcff0546e99e8373901c5a910ac.png)

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
w_1 =\dfrac{1}{2} - 2 w_2 .
$$

The variable $w_2$ is a free variable. Setting $w_2 = 0,$  we get $w_1 = \dfrac{1}{2},$ and therefore
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/726b5737809539337c1a8a259727a47b9bdacdf81de92a4a35783518df9dcaa0.png)

Therefore, the general solution is given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/a1a3e46d8352ceee549fb5040261d8edf036d8fb32fc5fc5b960cab07097970f.png)

Now, we need to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial condition ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14067736/assets/2e3a20e62437546fb2498d1575c9ed2cd268c43b968174ea7e0139977fb6fbd5.png) Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}-2([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]t{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(4t-3){e}^{3t} \\ (1-2t){e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The system decouples into x₁′=x₁/2 and x₂′=x₂/2. Thus each component is an arbitrary constant times e^{t/2}, giving option e.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]x(t).$
after.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t/2}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t/2},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Question 1
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[120012]x(t).

a
 x(t)=c1[10]e−t/2+c2[01]et/2,c1,c2∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]e−t/2+c2[01]e−t/2,c1,c2∈R
c
 x(t)=c1[10]et+c2[01]et,c1,c2∈R
d
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e2t,c1,c2∈R
e
x(t)=c1[10]et/2+c2[01]et/2,c1,c2∈R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]et/2+c2[01]et/2,c1,c2∈R.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case
content.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]x(t).$
content.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t/2}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t/2},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Question 2
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[1.7001.7]x(t).

a
x(t)=c1[10]e1.7t+c2[01]e−1.7t,c1,c2∈R
b
x(t)=c1[10]e1.7t+c2[01]e1.7t,c1,c2∈R
c
x(t)=c1[10]e−1.7tc1∈R
d
x(t)=c1[10]e1.7t,c1∈R
e
x(t)=c1[10]te1.7t+c2[10]e1.7t,c1,c2∈R
Submit

decision.explanation: Both components satisfy xᵢ′(t)=1.7xᵢ(t), so xᵢ(t)=cᵢe^{1.7t}. Option b includes both independent arbitrary constants and therefore gives the general solution.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1.7 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.7\end{aligned}]x(t).$
after.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{1.7t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{1.7t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Question 2
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[1.7001.7]x(t).

a
x(t)=c1[10]e1.7t+c2[01]e−1.7t,c1,c2∈R
b
x(t)=c1[10]e1.7t+c2[01]e1.7t,c1,c2∈R
c
x(t)=c1[10]e−1.7tc1∈R
d
x(t)=c1[10]e1.7t,c1∈R
e
x(t)=c1[10]te1.7t+c2[10]e1.7t,c1,c2∈R
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form [x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e1.7t+c2[01]e1.7t,c1,c2∈R.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option b: each component independently satisfies xᵢ′=1.7xᵢ, giving two arbitrary constants multiplying e^{1.7t}. Option d omits solutions with a nonzero second component.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case
content.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1.7 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.7\end{aligned}]x(t).$
content.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{1.7t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{1.7t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Question 3
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[100010]x(t).

a
 x(t)=c1[10]e−10tc1∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]e10t+c2[01]e−10t,c1,c2∈R
c
 x(t)=c1[10]e10t+c2[01]te10t,c1,c2∈R
d
x(t)=c1[10]e10t+c2[01]e10t,c1,c2∈R
e
 x(t)=c1[10]e10t,c1∈R
Submit

decision.explanation: The system decouples into x₁′=10x₁ and x₂′=10x₂. Each component is an independent arbitrary constant times e^{10t}, so option d gives the general solution.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]x(t).$
after.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{10t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{10t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Question 3
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[100010]x(t).

a
 x(t)=c1[10]e−10tc1∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]e10t+c2[01]e−10t,c1,c2∈R
c
 x(t)=c1[10]e10t+c2[01]te10t,c1,c2∈R
d
x(t)=c1[10]e10t+c2[01]e10t,c1,c2∈R
e
 x(t)=c1[10]e10t,c1∈R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e10t+c2[01]e10t,c1,c2∈R.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case
content.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]x(t).$
content.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{10t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{10t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Question 4
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[2002]x(t).

a
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t,c1∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e−2t,c1,c2∈R
c
 x(t)=c1[10]e−2tc1∈R
d
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]te2t,c1,c2∈R
e
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e2t,c1,c2∈R
Submit

decision.explanation: Both components satisfy xᵢ′=2xᵢ, so each equals an independent arbitrary constant times e^{2t}. Option e therefore gives the general solution.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t).$
after.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Question 4
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[2002]x(t).

a
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t,c1∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e−2t,c1,c2∈R
c
 x(t)=c1[10]e−2tc1∈R
d
 x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]te2t,c1,c2∈R
e
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e2t,c1,c2∈R
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[01]e2t,c1,c2∈R.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option e. Both components independently satisfy xᵢ′=2xᵢ, so the general solution requires two arbitrary constants multiplying e^{2t}. Option a omits all solutions with a nonzero second component.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case
content.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t).$
content.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

decision.explanation: The system decouples into x₁′=(2/3)x₁ and x₂′=(2/3)x₂. Each component equals an independent arbitrary constant times e^{2t/3}, giving option e.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]x(t).$
after.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t/3}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t/3},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Question 5
?

Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation x′(t)=[230023]x(t).

a
 x(t)=c1[10]e−2t/3+c2[01]e−2t/3,c1,c2∈R
b
 x(t)=c1[10]e3t/2+c2[01]e3t/2,c1,c2∈R
c
 x(t)=c1[10]e−2t/3+c2[01]e2t/3,c1,c2∈R
d
 x(t)=c1[10]e−3t/2+c2[01]e3t/2,c1,c2∈R
e
x(t)=c1[10]e2t/3+c2[01]e2t/3,c1,c2∈R
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

[x1′(t)x2′(t)]=[λ00λ][x1(t)x2(t)], the formula for the general solution is x(t)=c1[10]eλt+c2[01]eλt,c1,c2∈R.

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled.

Therefore, the general solution is given by x(t)=c1[10]e2t/3+c2[01]e2t/3,c1,c2∈R.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Complete Case
content.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]x(t).$
content.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t/3}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t/3},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

before.name: Question 6
before.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$

decision.explanation: With λ=-1, (A+I)[a,1]ᵀ=[0,3a]ᵀ=0, so a=0. The generalized eigenvector satisfies (A+I)[b,0]ᵀ=[0,1]ᵀ, giving 3b=1. Thus a+b=1/3.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1-(-1) & 0 \\ 3 & -1-(-1)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 3{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=\frac{1}{3},$ and $a+b=\frac{1}{3}.$

content.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1-(-1) & 0 \\ 3 & -1-(-1)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 3{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-1.$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}1+1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3+1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{w}_{1}+4{w}_{2}=-2 \\ -1{w}_{1}-2{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-1-2{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=-1,$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=-2,b=-1,$ and $a+b=-3.$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Defective Case
content.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-1.$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}1+1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3+1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{w}_{1}+4{w}_{2}=-2 \\ -1{w}_{1}-2{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-1-2{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=-1,$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=-2,b=-1,$ and $a+b=-3.$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ a\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ a\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-3t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ b\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,

what is the value of $a+b?$
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-3+3 & 5 \\ 0 & -3+3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+5{w}_{2}=1 \\ 0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{1}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{1}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-3t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=\frac{1}{5},$ and $a+b=\frac{1}{5}.$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{2t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =2$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}2-2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 1{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{2t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=1,$ and $a+b=1.$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ a\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ a\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-2.$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1+2 & -1 \\ 1 & -3+2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}-{w}_{2}=1 \\ {w}_{1}-{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is the same as the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}={w}_{2}+1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=1,$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=1,b=1,$ and $a+b=2.$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−1−11−3].

We are given that the eigenvalue is λ=−2 (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get A−λI=[1−11−1]∼[1−100]. So, we get an eigenvector v=[11].

To find w, we solve the equation (A−λI)w=v as follows:

(A−λI)w=v[−1+2−11−3+2][w1w2]=[11][1−11−1][w1w2]=[11]

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations: {w1−w2=1w1−w2=1

Note that the first equation is the same as the second. So, we obtain w1=w2+1.

The variable w2 is a free variable. Setting w2=0, we get w1=1, and therefore w=[10].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Defective Case
content.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ a\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ a\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-2.$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1+2 & -1 \\ 1 & -3+2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}-{w}_{2}=1 \\ {w}_{1}-{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is the same as the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}={w}_{2}+1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=1,$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=1,b=1,$ and $a+b=2.$

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-2+2 & 0 \\ 5 & -2+2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 5{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{c}_{2}}{5} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{c}_{2}}{5} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}. \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} \\ (2+5t){e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-2+2 & 0 \\ 5 & -2+2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 5{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{c}_{2}}{5} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{c}_{2}}{5} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}. \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} \\ (2+5t){e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let N=A+I=[−6,−4;9,6]. Since N²=0, x(t)=e^{-t}(I+tN)x(0). Here Nx(0)=[−10,15]ᵀ, giving x(t)=[(1−10t)e^{-t},(1+15t)e^{-t}]ᵀ, which is option d.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -4 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-1.$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -4 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-7+1 & -4 \\ 9 & 5+1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-6{w}_{1}-4{w}_{2}=-2 \\ 9{w}_{1}+6{w}_{2}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get ${w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3},$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+5([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 15\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(1-10t){e}^{-t} \\ (1+15t){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem in a Defective Case
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -4 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-1.$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -4 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-7+1 & -4 \\ 9 & 5+1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-6{w}_{1}-4{w}_{2}=-2 \\ 9{w}_{1}+6{w}_{2}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get ${w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3},$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+5([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 15\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(1-10t){e}^{-t} \\ (1+15t){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 13
?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−3−60−3]x(t),x(0)=[12].

a
[(1−12t)e−3t2e−3t]
b
[(1−12t)e−3t(2−12t)e−3t]
c
[e−3t(2−12t)e−3t]
d
[e−3t2e−3t]
e
[(1+t)e−3t(2−12t)e−3t]
Submit

decision.explanation: The second equation gives x₂(t)=2e^{-3t}. Then x₁′+3x₁=−12e^{-3t}, so (e^{3t}x₁)′=−12. Using x₁(0)=1 gives x₁(t)=(1−12t)e^{-3t}, matching option a.
